title: Scratchpad Patching: Decoupling Compute from Patch Size in Byte-Level Language Models
claim: Standard patch models refresh context only once per patch; inserting transient intermediate states inside patches keeps context fresh without adding committed states.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right with arrow; byte rows sandwiching a central trunk block
description: Two side-by-side panels joined by a blue arrow, both showing the byte string 'The_post-token_era'. Each panel has a row of byte boxes at the bottom and top, with a wide green 'Main Trunk' block in the middle. Bytes are color-coded by patch (gray, teal, yellow, purple). In the left panel, one solid circular node per patch aggregates its bytes via fan-in lines, feeds the trunk, and the trunk outputs one node per patch that fans out to predict the following bytes. In the right panel, many dashed circles (transient scratchpads) are inserted at extra byte positions alongside the solid patch nodes. They aggregate bytes seen so far and feed the trunk, and trunk outputs refresh predictions at many more positions. The dense line mesh in the right panel draws the eye first.
caption: Scratchpad Patching (SP). Left: a standard patch-based byte-level model runs the trunk M once per patch (see Fig. 2 for the full architecture), leaving most byte predictions to rely on a stale representation from the previous patch. Right: SP inserts transient scratchpads at selected byte positions, each aggregating the bytes seen so far within the patch and refreshing the trunk representation for subsequent predictions. This reduces patch lag while leaving the number of committed patch states unchanged. Other architectural components are omitted for clarity.
abstract: Tokenizer-free language models eliminate the tokenizer step of the language modeling pipeline by operating directly on bytes; patch-based variants further aggregate contiguous byte spans into patches for efficiency. However, the average patch size chosen at the model design stage governs a tight trade-off: larger patches reduce compute and KV-cache footprint, but degrade modeling quality. We trace this trade-off to patch lag: until a patch is fully observed, byte predictions within it must rely on a stale representation from the previous patch to preserve causality; this lag widens as patches grow larger. We introduce Scratchpad Patching (SP), which inserts transient scratchpads inside each patch to aggregate the bytes seen so far and refresh patch-level context for subsequent predictions. SP triggers scratchpads using next-byte prediction entropy, selectively allocating compute to information-dense regions and enabling post-hoc adjustment of inference-time compute. Across experiments on natural language and code, SP improves model quality at the same patch size; for example, even at $16$ bytes per patch, SP-augmented models match or closely approach the byte-level baseline on downstream evaluations while using a $16\times$ smaller KV-cache over patches and requiring roughly $3$-$4\times$ less inference compute than the byte-level baseline.
